question.text:
Given the matrices \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

in which of the following expressions is the Hadamard product well-defined?

  1. $B^TA \odot B\,\text{diag}(\mathbf{v})$
  2. $A \odot B\mathbf{v}^T$
  3. $AB \odot B\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{v}$
Hint: Here, $\text{diag}(\mathbf{v})$ is a diagonal matrix with the entries of $\mathbf{v}$ on the diagonal.
question.explanation:
The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

First, notice that $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times3$ matrix, and $\mathbf{v}$ is a $1\times3$ row vector.

Now, let's consider each expression in turn:

  • The dimensions of $B^T A$ are $3\times2,$ and the dimensions of $B\,\text{diag}(\mathbf{v})$ are $2\times3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is not well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $A$ are $2\times2,$ and the dimensions of $B\mathbf{v}^T$ are $2\times1.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is not well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $AB$ are $2\times3,$ and the dimensions of $B\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{v}$ are $2\times3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

example.title: Determining Whether a Matrix Expression Involving the Hadamard Product is Well-Defined

question.text: Given that \[ X \odot Y = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \quad Z = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad \alpha = 3 \] find $(\alpha Y) \odot X +Z^T.$
question.explanation:
For compatible matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ and scalar $\alpha,$ the Hadamard product has the following properties:

  • Commutativity: \[ A \odot B = B \odot A \]

  • Associativity: \[ (A \odot B) \odot C = A \odot (B \odot C) \]

  • Distributivity over Addition: \[ A \odot (B + C) = A \odot B + A \odot C \]

  • Scalar Distributivity: \[ \alpha (A \odot B) = (\alpha A) \odot B = A \odot (\alpha B) \]

In this case, by the scalar distributivity of the Hadamard product, we have \[ (\alpha Y) \odot X +Z^T= \alpha (Y \odot X) +Z^T. \]

Then, by the commutativity of the Hadamard product, we have

\begin{align*} \alpha (Y \odot X) +Z^T &= \alpha (X \odot Y) +Z^T\\[5pt] &= 3\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 \\ 4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}^T \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ -9 & 12 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6-5 & -3+4 \\ -9+2 & 12-3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -7 & 9 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:

A = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 3 \\ -1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Given the matrices above, write $A\mathbf{x}^T \odot (\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{x}^T)$ as a matrix product.

question.explanation:
The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ can be expressed as the matrix product \[ \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{u} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{v})\mathbf{u}. \]

In our case, we have \[ A\mathbf{x}^T = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 3 \\ -1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \] and \[ \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{x}^T = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Notice that they are of the same size; hence, their Hadamard product is well-defined. We conclude that \begin{align*} A\mathbf{x}^T \odot (\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{x}^T) &= \text{diag}(A\mathbf{x}^T)(\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{x}^T) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{8} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that \[ A \odot B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad C = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \] find $C^T + B \odot A.$
question.explanation:
For compatible matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ and scalar $\alpha,$ the Hadamard product has the following properties:

  • Commutativity: \[ A \odot B = B \odot A \]

  • Associativity: \[ (A \odot B) \odot C = A \odot (B \odot C) \]

  • Distributivity over Addition: \[ A \odot (B + C) = A \odot B + A \odot C \]

  • Scalar Distributivity: \[ \alpha (A \odot B) = (\alpha A) \odot B = A \odot (\alpha B) \]

In this case, by the commutativity of the Hadamard product, we have \begin{align*} C^T + B \odot A &= C^T + A \odot B \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^T + \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
